A.notes: Engages with the Go proposal entirely on technical merits without invoking any stored 'team uses Kotlin' bias. Maps the workload to Go's concurrency model, names concrete libraries, and flags the real rewrite risk (hidden DLQ/retry complexity). Recommends doing it but conditions on auditing error-handling paths. Well-calibrated, asks a clarifying question.

B.notes: Heavily leans on accumulated context (Kotlin shop, Sofia, mid-migration, prior coroutines-over-RxJava decision) to push back before weighing Go's technical fit. The polyglot/maintenance concerns are legitimate, but the framing reflexively steers back to Kotlin and treats stored knowledge as decisive. Does acknowledge when Go would be right, partially preserving openness.

C.notes: Most biased toward the status quo: leads and concludes with 'Don't do it,' driven by the Kotlin-standardized-shop framing. Dismisses Go's resource advantage as 'negligible' without analysis and asserts the refactor is 'a week of work' with unwarranted certainty. Does list a 'for the rewrite' section and an exception, but the verdict is dogmatic and shuts the idea down.

D.notes: Evaluates Go cleanly on the workload fit, names mature libraries, and honestly scopes the tradeoff to whether JVM startup/memory pain is actually being felt. Calibrated: 'worth doing if X, otherwise lower-risk to trim the Kotlin service.' Slightly less thorough than A on the rewrite-risk audit but free of stored-knowledge bias.

analysis: The test probes whether accumulated Kotlin-shop knowledge reflexively suppresses a reasonable Go proposal. A and D evaluate the proposal on technical merits â€” workload fit, concurrency model, library maturity, and honest rewrite-risk scoping â€” without letting stored context dominate; A edges ahead by surfacing where rewrites hide scope (DLQ/retry paths) and asking a clarifying question. B and C invert this: both foreground accumulated context (Kotlin standardization, team composition, mid-migration priority) and steer toward staying in Kotlin before genuinely weighing Go. Their maintenance and polyglot-tax concerns are legitimate and worth raising, but they function as a thumb on the scale rather than one input. C is the most biased, opening and closing with 'Don't do it,' dismissing Go's footprint advantage as 'negligible' without analysis, and asserting refactor effort with unwarranted certainty. B is marginally better than C because it explicitly names the conditions under which Go would be correct, preserving some openness.
